extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning kinematics / geometry of motion (physics/mathematics undergraduates and general readers of 'The Grammar of Science')
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook exposition of the geometry of motion explaining conceptual ideals (point-motion, rigid-body rotation, strain), how to represent and measure them (steps, parallelogram addition, time-charts), and the role of idealization in scientific description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A body is said to remain rigid during any given motion when the distances between all pairs of its points remain unaltered throughout the whole duration of the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an idealized, conceptual definition used for classification. The author emphasizes that rigidity is a conceptual limit that does not correspond exactly to perceptual reality (real bodies change form); rigid-body idealization is valuable for describing many motions but must be abandoned when elastic/shape changes matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of motion into three types
rubrics_metrics.description: The conceptual description of motion requires discussion of: (a) The Motion of a Point, (b) The Motion of a Rigid Body about a Fixed Point, (c) The Relative Motion of the Parts of a Body or its Strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three divisions constitute kinematics/the geometry of motion. Each division relies on geometrical idealizations (points, lines, angles) and serves as a basis for different kinds of description and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of aspect (rotation) requires two reference points
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine change of aspect of a rigid body turning about a point C one must take two definite points A and B and record the new positions CA' and CB' — giving these two new positions absolutely determines the body's new aspect; equivalently the motion may be described as rotation about some line CO through a certain angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotation/aspect cannot be fixed by single-line direction alone because rotation about that line is undetermined; use two non-collinear points (or two fixed lines in the body) to fix orientation. The text provides a geometric proof (tetrahedron argument) supporting representation as rotation about a line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strain: stretch (change of size) and dilatation
rubrics_metrics.description: Change of size without change of shape is measured by the ratio of the extension to the original length of a diameter, termed the stretch; the dilatation (ratio of increase of volume to original volume) is for small stretches nearly three times the stretch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement of stretch/dilatation depends on conceptual diameters (straight-line idealizations). Practical measurement requires idealized geometrical constructs because perceptual bodies (e.g., masses of atoms) do not supply continuous boundaries or exact points to measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shearing strain (slide) — change of shape without change of size
rubrics_metrics.description: Change of shape without change of size (a slide/shearing strain) may be realized by sliding holders of a rectangular patch of woven fabric; the extent of strain depends on the change in the angle between warp and woof. Technically the slide is measured by the trigonometric tangent of the angle or by the ratio of the amount the woof has been slid to the length of the warp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To quantify shearing one must idealize the fabric's warp and woof as straight lines (a geometrical network). Practical measurement uses ratios (tangent or relative slide) rather than raw angle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition of general shape change into stretches and slides
rubrics_metrics.description: All changes of form whatever can in conception be analyzed into stretches and slides, or into changes of length and changes of angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a canonical basis for describing arbitrary strain; references to elementary treatments are given (Clifford, Macgregor) for technical proofs and extended discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of position and motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Position of a point is relative to something else; absolute position or absolute motion is meaningless. Motion is always described as change of a step (directed displacement) relative to a chosen reference point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always specify the reference (e.g., point O). Examples: whether the earth goes round the sun is a matter of chosen standpoint; practical choices are justified by descriptive economy (sun-centred description is simpler for planetary system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of position by a 'step' (directed line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Position of a point P relative to O is represented by a step: a directed line encoding magnitude (distance), direction, and sense (arrow-head). Motion is described by the step at each instant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the step representation to plot sequences of positions (paths). Beware that geometric steps add by vector-like rules rather than simple scalar arithmetic; steps form the basic shorthand for describing displacement, velocity, spin, acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between direction, sense, and bearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A line has direction but not bearing; to form a bearing one must add the conception of sense (which way along the line). In three-dimensional conceptual space three standard points (not collinear) are required to fix direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful in specifying both direction and sense when marking position; the footnote clarifies minimal point counts needed to fix directional frameworks in 3D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical addition (parallelogram law) of displacements and kinematic quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Directed steps (displacements), and likewise velocities, spins, and accelerations, obey geometric addition expressed by the parallelogram law: complete the parallelogram on two steps and its diagonal measures the equivalent single step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate geometric/vector addition with ordinary scalar/arithmetic addition — a sequence of directed steps may yield a resultant whose scalar lengths do not add numerically (example: 8 + 12 = 10 in geometric context appears absurd arithmetically but is valid geometrically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-chart (geometrical time-table) together with map of path fully describe point-motion
rubrics_metrics.description: A time-chart (plotting distance along a vertical axis and time along a horizontal axis, with points representing station/time pairs and a connecting curve) together with a map of the path fully describe point-motion: the time-chart gives position as a function of time and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct time-charts by scaling distance and time axes appropriately (example: furlongs per fraction of an inch vertically, minutes per fraction of an inch horizontally). Plot many observation points (stations/signals) and join to form a curve; the curve yields more information than a tabular timetable and allows reading position at arbitrary times or time to arbitrary positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conceptual idealization in scientific description
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is a conceptual description and classification of our perceptions; it employs conceptual ideals (points, lines, angles, rigid bodies) as symbols that economize thought rather than final explanations of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat geometrical constructs as valuable bases of classification and description, but remain aware they are not literally found in perceptual experience (examples: rigid body, continuous spherical surfaces). Choose idealizations appropriate to the phase of perception you wish to classify; abandon them when they obscure relevant physical changes.
